title: The S&P 500 will surge 23% by the end of 2027, Deutsche Bank predicts
excerpt: It's been a rocky stretch for stocks. But even as volatility is expected to continue next year, Deutsche Bank predicts the S&P 500 will rally to 9,000.
content_html:
What sell-off? A top bank says stocks will surge 23% by the end of next year.

By Madeline Berg

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-27T19:00:57.606Z

It's been a rocky stretch for markets, but investors should stay upbeat heading into 2027.

Despite fears of a deepening AI sell-off derailing the bull market after a series of brutal routs, Deutsche Bank has very bullish target for year-end 2027.

In its outlook for the coming year, the bank predicts that while the market could be in for some additional near-term pain, the S&P 500 will reach 9,000 by the end of 2027, a surge of 23% from Friday's close.

And even though tech jitters are running high these days, the bank's analysts say the 2027 rally will be largely driven by AI.

"We remain firmly of the view that AI will have a significant productivity impact, and the evidence is becoming more supportive: AI-related capex is already large enough to influence US growth, while early signs point to stronger productivity in more AI-intensive sectors," the analysts wrote.

AI-related spending, including capital expenditures and consumer spending, is set to continue to grow next year. Real growth in equipment spending will sit at about 10%, the bank predicts.

And AI-related productivity gains will lead to strong earnings. The output per hour of nonfarm workers has grown by 2% to 2.5%, the bank said, and will continue to grow over the next two years. Gains in the job market, including across construction and manufacturing, will also boost the economy, as will lower energy prices.

Any slump along the way, like the streak of selling in recent weeks, is a necessary step on the way toward "the promised land," the bank said, noting that the US economy has been largely resilient despite hiccups this year.

"Overinvestment, busts and unexpected winners and losers are part of the journey," researchers Jim Reid and David Folkerts-Landau wrote.

Those bumps in the road could be the result of inflation, overinvestment in AI, or geopolitics, such as the war in Ukraine, increased competition from China, or threats to the Middle Eastern energy supply.

Despite the recent volatility, the stock market remains positive for this year. The S&P 500 has climbed more than 6.5% year to date, while the Nasdaq 100 is up 5%.

"If our great expectations are fulfilled, 2027 could ultimately be a very good year. But don't expect it to feel like that every day in what is likely to be another volatile year," the Deutsche Bank analysts wrote.
